the Neoarchean crustal growth of the North China Craton occurred through the following processes: (1) the accretion of the juvenile crust by the subduction of the depleted mantle and the thickening of the alkali-rich juvenile crust, (2) the reworking of the crustal materials by the remelting, and (3) the underplating of the crust by the magma upwelling of the depleted mantle source.

the Neoarchean crustal accretions in the eastern North Chinese craton occurred at ca. 2 Ga, and the crustal evolution in the craton was characterized by a major crustal thickening event at ca. 3 Ga followed by a series of crustal accretional and reworking events at ca. 2700 Ma, 2550-2480 Ma, and 2500 Ma, respectively.

the North China Craton has been the product of the Neoarchean crustal accretions and reworking, and the Neoarchean tephrochronology and tectono-geological history of the eastern North China Craton have been well constrained.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the North China cratonic crust was not assembled in one single event, but instead was built up in a series of accretionary and underplating events.
crustal reworking by magma upwelled from the depleted mantle source is an important mechanism for the formation of the continental crust.
the Neoarchean tides of the North China Craton were driven by mantle-plume activity and crustal accretions, which led to the growth of continental crust and the formation of cratons.
